citation: Bauer, Bottenbruch, Läuchli, Penzlin, Rutishauser and Samelson (19 Oct 1957). Letter from GAMM members to John Carr III, President of the ACM. Reproduced in English in Bemer, R. W. (1969). A Politico-Social History of Algol. Annual Review in Automatic Programming 5, log-book item [2], pp. 160-161.
quote: We have endeavored from the beginning to avoid the possibility of deviations from existing earlier proposals (Rutishauser 1951, FORTRAN, partly also PACT).
what: the European (GAMM) proposal that went into ALGOL 58 was deliberately kept close to earlier proposals, FORTRAN named among them
reason: Best positive primary sentence found: the European designers themselves say they tried not to deviate from FORTRAN (one of three named predecessors). Read from the text layer of the scanned PDF (OCR, sentence clean). It is the designers' letter, in Bemer's English rendering, inside a compilation; it concerns the GAMM proposal of 1957, i.e. the road to ALGOL 58, not ALGOL 60 directly. The same letter adds that their proposals 'largely agree structurally with Perlis' IT language and the Remington-Rand Math-Matic', so FORTRAN is one predecessor among several.

citation: Perlis, A. J. and Samelson, K. (1958). Preliminary Report: International Algebraic Language. Communications of the ACM 1(12), 8-22.
quote: On the other hand the ACM proposal was based on experience with several successful, working problem oriented languages.
what: the American (ACM) proposal drew on experience with existing working languages (not named in the sentence; FORTRAN, IT and MATH-MATIC were the working American ones)
reason: Primary and positive, but FORTRAN is not named, so it supports the tie only indirectly. Read from the text layer of the scan.

citation: Perlis, A. J. (1978/1981). The American Side of the Development of ALGOL. HOPL I (ACM SIGPLAN Notices 13(8); Wexelblat, ed., History of Programming Languages, Academic Press), pp. 75-91, incl. session transcript.
quote: ALGOL 58 was based on a model strongly derived from FORTRAN
what: ALGOL 58's model (scalar arithmetic processing) derived from FORTRAN
reason: NOT VERIFIED. The wording comes only from search-engine summaries of the ACM PDF (which add that it was therefore oriented toward scalar arithmetic processing); the ACM Digital Library returned 403 to WebFetch and a bot check in the browser, and no free copy was found (Caltech record is metadata only). The PDF covers the whole ALGOL session (Perlis paper, Naur paper, transcripts), so even the speaker is unconfirmed. If confirmed in the printed text, this would be the strongest sentence for the tie. Needs a human to open the PDF at the DOI.

citation: Bauer, F. L. and Samelson, K. (1959). The problem of a common language, especially for scientific numeral work. Proc. International Conference on Information Processing (ICIP), UNESCO, Paris, pp. 120-125.
quote: Most of these requirements are met already, at least partially, by previous attempts, such as FORTRAN and MATH-MATIC.
what: FORTRAN as an earlier attempt that already met part of the goals set for the common language
reason: Precedent only: two of the European designers name FORTRAN as a previous attempt, without saying anything was taken. OCR text (one stray period in 'requirem.ents' removed). The abstract of the same paper also says: 'A common language should be, like FORTRAN, an operational, constructive language' (comparison, not borrowing).

citation: IBM reply (Mar 1961) to an open letter from Rene De La Briandais to R. W. Bemer in Communications of the ACM. Quoted in Bemer, R. W. (1969). A Politico-Social History of Algol. Annual Review in Automatic Programming 5, log-book item [67], pp. 179-180.
quote: Although ALGOL is admittedly a superior language (it should be, for IBM's own FORTRAN and experimental languages made heavy contributions), FORTRAN is the present workhorse and is operative in a large number of installations
what: 'heavy contributions' of FORTRAN to ALGOL (unspecified)
reason: A contemporary statement that names FORTRAN as a heavy contributor to ALGOL, but it is IBM's (presumably Bemer's) public reply in a dispute over why IBM did not ship ALGOL, not an ALGOL designer's account, and it is self-interested. The log entry does not name the reply's author. Text layer of the scan.

citation: Bright, H. (1961), remark at the RAND Symposium, as reported in Datamation (Sep 1961). Quoted in Bemer, R. W. (1969). A Politico-Social History of Algol, log-book item [75].
quote: I think people are ignoring the fact that FORTRAN represented a giant step and ALGOL represents a refinement, a generalization, and a maturing.
what: ALGOL as a refinement and generalization of the step FORTRAN took
reason: A contemporary observer, not a designer. Bemer answers in the same exchange: 'FORTRAN wasn't really such a giant step as far as the language was concerned. This had been done by both Rutishauser and Laning and Zierler at MIT many years before', which cuts the other way.

citation: de Beer, H. T. (2006). The History of the ALGOL Effort. Master thesis, Eindhoven University of Technology, sections 1.2.2 and 1.3 (citing Rosen 1967, p. 10).
quote: Exactly this dominance was the reason for the American subcommittee to ignore the existence of FORTRAN. Choosing FORTRAN as basis for their proposal would only increase the dominant position of IBM.
what: FORTRAN deliberately not chosen as the basis of the American proposal
reason: CUTS THE OTHER WAY. A historian's reading: 'Both the Americans and the Europeans did not base their proposal on an already existing language' and 'the Americans wanted to undermine the dominance of IBM'. The thesis has no Perlis sentence about FORTRAN as a model. It does note that the FORTRAN and IAL preliminary reports 'resemble each other' in how they describe the language (resemblance of the documents).

citation: Backus, J. (1978/1981). The History of FORTRAN I, II and III. HOPL I.
quote: My own opinion as to the effect of FORTRAN on later languages and the collective impact of such languages on programming generally is not a popular opinion.
what: none stated
reason: Full text searched (text layer): Backus never says ALGOL took anything from FORTRAN and does not discuss Zurich or the international language in this paper. He only groups 'the FORTRANs, the ALGOLs, their successors and derivatives' as von Neumann languages. Also checked, with no FORTRAN sentence in the text layer: Backus (1959) 'The syntax and semantics of the proposed international algebraic language' (ICIP) and the ACM Ad Hoc Committee proposal of 1958 (poor OCR). Not reachable: Naur's HOPL paper (ACM only), Knuth and Trabb Pardo (file too large or 403).

citation: Wirth, N. (1993). Recollections about the Development of Pascal. HOPL II, ACM SIGPLAN Notices 28(3), 333-342.
quote: The form of COBOL-like record types was due to Hoare, as well as the idea to represent a computer's "logical words" by a well-known abstraction, namely sets (of small integers).
what: record types, COBOL-like in form, reaching Pascal through Hoare's proposals
reason: Wirth calls Pascal's record types 'COBOL-like' and credits their form to Hoare. Read in full in the browser from a retyped HTML copy of the paper (the site has small transcription slips such as 'CAR. Hoare', hence medium); the ACM original was not reachable.

citation: Wirth, N. (1993). Recollections about the Development of Pascal. HOPL II, ACM SIGPLAN Notices 28(3), 333-342.
quote: the addition of basic data types for double precision real numbers and for complex numbers was proposed, as well as the record structure known from COBOL
what: step 1 of the chain: the record structure 'known from COBOL' proposed for the ALGOL successor (the Wirth and Hoare proposal that became ALGOL W)
reason: Chain: COBOL records -> Hoare's record proposal -> ALGOL W -> Pascal. This sentence gives COBOL -> ALGOL W proposal; the same paper says 'the basic framework of Pascal stems from Algol W'. A third sentence: Pascal introduced 'new forms of structuring: record, set, and file (sequence), several of which had been present in COBOL' (precedent wording). Search summaries also report a line from the HOPL II presentation transcript, that Pascal inherited the record structure from COBOL indirectly via Hoare's proposal in ALGOL W; that wording was not seen directly.

citation: Hoare, C. A. R. (1965). Record Handling. ALGOL Bulletin 21, section 3.6, pp. 39-69; Wirth, N. and Hoare, C. A. R. (1966). A Contribution to the Development of ALGOL. Communications of the ACM 9(6), 413-432.
quote: The idea that the reference structure of the data should be placed entirely under the control of the programmer is a most important contribution of AED-O, and is taken over in this proposal.
what: Hoare's 1965 record proposal credits AED-0 (Ross) and McCarthy, not COBOL, in its text layer
reason: No sentence naming COBOL was found in the OCR text of either document (scans; a COBOL mention could be lost to OCR, e.g. in Hoare's comparison section 5). Wirth and Hoare (1966) says only: 'the replacement of tree structures by records as proposed by the second author'. So the COBOL credit rests on Wirth's 1993 recollection.

citation: Meertens, L. (2022). The Origins of Python. Inference: International Review of Science 7(3).
quote: A precursor can be found in Peter Landin's ISWIM, a suite of gedankenexperiment languages that used optional indentation, not for readability, but mirroring its use in mathematics.
what: indentation for grouping: ISWIM named only as a precursor
reason: ABC's designer names ISWIM as a precursor, not a source. In the same passage he gives the actual source: P. J. Plauger's article 'Signal and Noise in Programming Languages' and its idea to 'let the indenting control grouping', 'a suggestion we followed with enthusiasm'. Quote assembled from two consecutive fetched segments (hence medium). By the inclusion rule this is precedent: no tie.

citation: van Rossum, G. (2011). Karin Dewar, Indentation and the Colon. The History of Python (blog), quoting an email from Lambert Meertens.
quote: The origin of indentation in ABC is thus simply the desire to have the program text look neat
what: indentation: Meertens' own account gives no ISWIM origin
reason: CUTS THE OTHER WAY. Meertens: mandatory indentation was there in B0 for neatness, 'codifying what was already common practice', and 'may have been influenced by [PL75]' (Plauger 1975). ISWIM, Landin and the off-side rule are not mentioned on the page. The 2019 CWI slides (image-only PDF) could not be read; a search summary says they list ISWIM (Landin 1966) and Plauger under the origins of indentation.

citation: Cantrill, B. (2009). A Conversation with Arthur Whitney. ACM Queue 7(2).
quote: Yes, at Morgan Stanley I did use the APL characters, but on my next iteration, K, which was in '92, I gave up on those characters.
what: K as the next iteration of Whitney's APL at Morgan Stanley (A+), dropping the APL character set
reason: The page itself stayed blocked (403 at queue.acm.org, cacm.acm.org and spawn-queue.acm.org, also in the browser). Two independent search summaries of the ACM copies reproduce the second half word for word ('but on my next iteration, K, which was in '92, I gave up on those characters') and paraphrase the first half consistently with the v2 quote, and report the nearby line 'I wrote an APL to do all of that'. So the v2 quote is very likely right but was not seen in full.

citation: Cooper, A. (1996). Why I am called 'the Father of Visual Basic'. cooper.com.
quote: Microsoft took advantage of this dynamic interface to unplug our little shell language and replace it entirely with QuickBasic.
what: Visual Basic's language is Microsoft's QuickBASIC, attached to Cooper's visual shell (Ruby)
reason: Essay not reachable: web.archive.org is blocked for the fetch tool and no other copy was found (Cooper's Medium repost returned 403). The wording comes from a search summary attributed to Cooper's essay, with a second line: 'convert it from a shell construction set for all users of Windows to a visual programming language for professional programmers by adding QuickBasic'. Unverified. Substance is product lineage (QuickBASIC is a BASIC), so the tie itself is safe; a human should open the Wayback URL to fix the wording. Secondary confirmation, also from a search summary only: the Computer History Museum says Microsoft paired Ruby with its QBasic language and released it as Visual Basic.

citation: Jazdzewski, C. (blog post, RemovingAllDoubt; reposted by Marco Cantu, Feb 2020, 'Chuck Jazdzewski on Delphi design').
quote: Create Visual Foo that would be more Visual than Visual Basic!
what: Delphi (first 'Visual Pascal') was conceived as Borland's answer to Visual Basic; the team reasoned that method pointers could do everything Visual Basic did
reason: The page timed out twice and failed in the browser; wording is from search summaries only (also: 'When TPW was released we received strong feedback from our users that Visual Basic was better and much easier to use'). Jazdzewski was Delphi's co-architect, so the source is primary, but what it shows is a target to beat plus an event model designed to match VB, not a plain statement that the form designer was copied. Not found: any Hejlsberg or Borland sentence saying Delphi took its form designer from VB. Hejlsberg (2019 interview, search summary) only says VB 'wasn't considered a grown-up' language; The Register (2020, secondary, read directly) says Delphi 'combined Object Pascal with a VB-like visual form builder'.

citation: SAP Community blog posts: 'ABAP - Past, Present, Future' (2021) and 'Evolution of ABAP' (2022). blogs.sap.com.
quote: syntax was heavily influenced by COBOL: keywords followed by parameters
what: statement syntax: keyword first, period at the end; MOVE, MOVE-CORRESPONDING, ADD-CORRESPONDING have COBOL counterparts
reason: No primary or official SAP statement found. blogs.sap.com returns 403; the wording is from search summaries (second post: ABAP 'borrowed some syntactical conventions from Cobol', and was also influenced by Software AG's Natural). Authors' standing at SAP not verified. SAP's own news article 'Celebrating ABAP: Programming Language Turns 40' (2023, read directly) does not mention COBOL at all. Wikipedia's COBOL entry for ABAP is tagged citation needed.

citation: IT History Society profile of Anthony J. Barr (ithistory.org); Barr, A. J. (2006). SAS History. barrsystems.com (Wayback only).
quote: Procedures were written in PL/1, while the systems and language portions were written in machine language.
what: SAS procedures were implemented in PL/I (nothing found on the language being modeled on PL/I)
reason: No Barr, Goodnight or SAS Institute sentence saying the SAS language was modeled on PL/I was found. Barr's own 'SAS History' page is 404 on the live site and only on web.archive.org (blocked). What is documented is implementation in PL/I (search summary, not read directly), which under the rule gives at most a weak non-design tie. The 'syntax inspired by PL/I' claim appears only in an unsourced DePaul course page.

citation: Odersky, M. et al. (2006). An Overview of the Scala Programming Language, Second Edition. EPFL Technical Report LAMP-REPORT-2006-001, section 10 (Related Work).
quote: Scala's abstract types have close resemblances to abstract types of signatures in the module systems of ML [24] and OCaml [29], generalizing them to a context of first-class components.
what: abstract types (as in ML module signatures)
reason: The sentence says 'close resemblances', but it stands in a list introduced by: 'Scala's design is influenced by many different languages and research papers. The following enumeration of related work lists the main design influences.' So influence by context, one type feature. PDF text extracted locally; 'fi/ff/fl' ligatures were dropped by the extractor and restored here ('first-class', 'different', 'influenced').

citation: Odersky, M. et al. (2006). An Overview of the Scala Programming Language, Second Edition. EPFL Technical Report LAMP-REPORT-2006-001, section 10.
quote: For-comprehensions are based on Haskell's monad comprehensions [46], even though their syntax more closely resembles XQuery [3]. Views have been influenced by Haskell's type classes [47].
what: for-comprehensions (from monad comprehensions) and views/implicits (from type classes)
reason: Direct statement, two named features. Strength is a judgment call: two features, one of them (implicits/type classes) central to Scala; weak proposed by the single-feature rule, strong is defensible. Ligature in 'influenced' restored.

citation: Odersky, M. et al. (2006). An Overview of the Scala Programming Language, Second Edition. EPFL Technical Report LAMP-REPORT-2006-001, section 10.
quote: Of course, Scala adopts a large part of the concepts and syntactic conventions of Java [23] and C# [15].
what: a large part of the concepts and syntactic conventions
reason: Extra candidate (check whether java -> scala is already recorded). Main parent by the authors' own words.

citation: Odersky, M. et al. (2006). An Overview of the Scala Programming Language, Second Edition. EPFL Technical Report LAMP-REPORT-2006-001, section 10.
quote: Of course, Scala adopts a large part of the concepts and syntactic conventions of Java [23] and C# [15].
what: concepts and syntactic conventions (named together with Java)
reason: Extra candidate. Named on equal terms with Java in the sentence; weak proposed because Java is the evident main parent (Scala also targeted .NET at the time).

citation: Odersky, M. et al. (2006). An Overview of the Scala Programming Language, Second Edition. EPFL Technical Report LAMP-REPORT-2006-001, section 10.
quote: From Smalltalk [22] comes the concept of a uniform object model.
what: uniform object model: every value an object, every operation a message send
reason: Extra candidate. Section 3 adds: 'Scala uses a pure object-oriented model similar to Smalltalk's: Every value is an object and every operation is a message send.'

citation: Odersky, M. et al. (2006). An Overview of the Scala Programming Language, Second Edition. EPFL Technical Report LAMP-REPORT-2006-001, section 10.
quote: Scala's abstract types have close resemblances to abstract types of signatures in the module systems of ML [24] and OCaml [29], generalizing them to a context of first-class components.
what: abstract types (module signatures)
reason: Extra candidate, same sentence and same caveat as ml -> scala ('close resemblances' inside the list of 'main design influences'). Elsewhere the paper treats OCaml as an alternative design ('OCaml and Moby are two alternative designs that combine functional and object-oriented programming'), so this one is borderline.

citation: Odersky, M. et al. (2006). An Overview of the Scala Programming Language, Second Edition. EPFL Technical Report LAMP-REPORT-2006-001, section 11 (Conclusion).
quote: Examples of this abound already in the Scala libraries and applications. There are classes to model Erlang style actors, arbitrary precision integers, Horn clauses and constraints, to name just three.
what: actor library modeled on Erlang-style actors
reason: Extra candidate, library route only. A stronger sentence is said to be in Odersky, Spoon and Venners, Programming in Scala, section 1.4 'Scala's roots' (actor library inspired by Erlang; uniform access principle from Eiffel), but artima.com returned 500/504, so it was not seen. Eiffel is NOT named in the Overview paper. Off-map influences named in section 10: Sather (properties), Beta (universal nesting), gbeta (virtual classes), Pizza ('Scala represents a continuation of the work on Pizza'), XQuery (syntax of for-comprehensions).

citation: Wolfram Research (n.d.). Wolfram Language FAQ: 'What languages were influences?'. wolfram.com.
quote: LISP and APL were two early influences, as was Stephen Wolfram's 1981 SMP symbolic computation language.
what: early design influence (unspecified in the sentence; symbolic expressions in Wolfram's other accounts)
reason: Official documentation, direct statement. Supporting, same author: Wolfram in an InfoQ podcast transcript, 'The languages that were probably the closest to being inspirations were probably LISP and APL.' (high); and in 'There Was a Time before Mathematica' (2013) he says of designing SMP that he knew 'ones like LISP and APL' (that essay does not state the borrowing in one sentence).

citation: Wolfram, S. (2012). Answer to a reader question on APL, J and K/q. Stephen Wolfram Q&A, stephenwolfram.com, 14 May 2012.
quote: I thought APL had some really interesting ideas, some of which have shown up in Mathematica.
what: 'some really interesting ideas' of APL (he studied APL in detail when designing SMP)
reason: The designer's own statement. The FAQ sentence in the lisp -> mathematica record ('LISP and APL were two early influences') supports this tie as well and is the more formal citation.

citation: ANSI X3.226-1994, Programming Language Common Lisp, section 1.1.2 History (as in the Common Lisp HyperSpec, K. Pitman ed., 1996).
quote: The major contributions of Scheme were lexical scoping, lexical closures, first-class continuations, and simplified syntax (no separation of value cells and function cells). Some of these contributions made a large impact on the design of Common Lisp.
what: lexical scoping and lexical closures
reason: Official standard text, fetched in consecutive segments. The same section also says: 'The primary influences on Common Lisp were Lisp Machine Lisp, MacLisp, NIL, S-1 Lisp, Spice Lisp, and Scheme.' Chapter 1 of Steele's 'Common Lisp the Language' (cs.cmu.edu node6) does not mention Scheme or lexical scoping at all, so it should not be the citation for this tie. The sentence says 'some of these contributions' without saying which; lexical scoping and closures are the ones Common Lisp has.
